slides.heading: ● Core Philosophy
bullets: ○ Effective agentic systems succeed by focusing on simplicity when possible
○ Success comes from proper system design and engineering,
○ Agents require balance: autonomy vs. safety, flexibility vs. reliability, power vs.
○ Building blocks: Clear instructions and robust tool definitions
○ Architectural patterns: When to use workflows vs. dynamic agents

slides.heading: ● Clear Prompts
bullets: ○ Use detailed instructions defining responsibilities, constraints, and boundaries
○ Specify when to use tools vs. when to escalate to humans
○ Use natural internet-text formats in prompts (markdown or XML)
○ Avoid abstract instructions, conflicting directives, or implicit assumptions -
always double check your prompt for these!

slides.heading: ● Simple Approaches First
bullets: ○ Single LLM calls with retrieval often sufficient for predefined, linear workflows

slides.heading: ● Workflows are great when:
bullets: ○ Tasks have known steps but require dynamic routing or parallelization
○ Iterative refinement loops with feedback are needed (reflection pattern)
○ You need structured execution paths with some LLM decision-making
○ Build workflows when your system requires a predictable structure with minor

slides.heading: ● Autonomous Agents are great for:
bullets: ○ Open-ended problems where steps cannot be predicted in advance
○ Systems requiring dynamic decision-making with multiple possible solution
○ Tasks requiring continuous adaptation and learning from outcomes
○ Exchange latency/cost for flexibility, but accept compounding error risks.

bullets: ● Input Guardrails: Reject prompt injection, verify types, check

slides.heading: Observability Essentials
bullets: ● Trace Capture: Log every prompt, response, tool call, and decision point
● Metrics: Track success/failure rates, latency, cost per operation, tool
● Error Analysis: Categorize errors, identify patterns, build recovery
